title: Of liberty of conscience
paragraphs: It is common to see good intentions, if carried on without moderation, push men into very vicious effects. In this dispute that has at present engaged France in a civil war, the better and sounder cause is no doubt the one that maintains the ancient religion and government of the kingdom. Nevertheless, among the good men of that party (for I am not speaking of those who only pretend to it, either to carry out their own private revenges, or gratify their avarice, or court the favour of princes, but of those who engage in the quarrel out of true zeal for religion and a holy desire to maintain the peace and government of their country) — of these, I say, we see many whom passion carries beyond the bounds of reason, and sometimes inspires with counsels that are unjust, violent, and even rash.

It is certain that in those first times, when our religion began to gain authority with the laws, zeal armed many against all kinds of pagan books, by which the learned suffered an excessive great loss — a disorder that I think did more damage to letters than all the flames of the barbarians. Cornelius Tacitus is very good testimony to this: for although the Emperor Tacitus, his kinsman, had by express order furnished all the libraries in the world with it, nevertheless one entire copy could not escape the searching examination of those who wanted to abolish it for the sake of only five or six idle clauses contrary to our belief.

They also had the trick of easily lending undue praises to all the emperors who favoured us, and of universally condemning all the actions of those who were our opponents — as is plainly seen in the Emperor Julian, surnamed the Apostate,

[The character of the Emperor Julian was censured, when Montaigne was at Rome in 1581, by the Master of the Sacred Palace, who, however, as Montaigne tells us in his journal (ii. 35), referred it to his conscience to alter what he should think in bad taste. Montaigne did not do so, and this chapter supplied Voltaire with the greater part of the praises he bestowed upon the Emperor. — Leclerc.]

who was, in truth, a very great and rare man, a man in whose soul philosophy was imprinted in the best characters, and by which he professed to govern all his actions; and in truth there is no sort of virtue of which he has not left notable examples. In chastity (of which his whole life gave manifest proof) we read the same of him as is said of Alexander and Scipio: being in the flower of his age, for he was killed by the Parthians at thirty-one, of a great many very beautiful captives he would not so much as look on one. As to his justice, he himself took the pains to hear the parties, and although he would out of curiosity inquire what religion they were of, the antipathy he had to ours never tilted the balance. He made several good laws himself, and repealed a large part of the subsidies and taxes levied by his predecessors.

We have two good historians who were eye-witnesses of his actions. One of them, Marcellinus, in several places of his history sharply reproves an edict of his that forbade all Christian rhetoricians and grammarians to keep school or to teach, and says he wishes that act of his had been buried in silence: it is probable that if he had done anything more severe against us, he, fond as he was of our party, would not have passed it over in silence. He was indeed sharp against us, but not a cruel enemy; for our own people tell this story of him: that one day, walking through the city of Chalcedon, Maris, bishop of the place, was bold enough to tell him that he was impious and an enemy to Christ — at which, they say, he was moved only to reply, "Go, poor wretch, and lament the loss of your eyes"; to which the bishop replied, "I thank Jesus Christ for taking away my sight, that I may not see your impudent face" — affecting in that, they say, a philosophical patience. But this action of his bears no comparison with the cruelty he is said to have practised on us. "He was," says Eutropius, my other witness, "an enemy to Christianity, but without putting his hand to blood." And to return to his justice, there is nothing he can be accused of in that, except the severity he exercised in the beginning of his reign against those who had followed the party of Constantius, his predecessor. As for his sobriety, he always lived a soldier's life, and observed a diet and routine like one who is preparing and steeling himself for the austerities of war. His vigilance was such that he divided the night into three or four parts, the least of which was given to sleep; the rest was spent either in visiting the state of his army and guards in person, or in study; for among other rare qualities he was very excellent in every kind of learning. It is said of Alexander the Great that in bed, for fear lest sleep should divert him from his thoughts and studies, he always had a basin set beside his bed, and held out one hand with a ball of copper in it, so that, as he started to fall asleep and his fingers let go, the ball falling into the basin would wake him. But the other had his soul so bent upon what he had a mind to do, and was so little troubled by fumes thanks to his unusual abstinence, that he had no need of any such invention. As to his military experience, he was excellent in all the qualities of a great captain, as he was likely to be, having spent almost all his life in a continual exercise of war, and most of that time with us in France against the Germans and Franks: we hardly read of any man who saw more dangers, or who gave more frequent proofs of his personal valour.

His death has something in it parallel with that of Epaminondas: for he was wounded with an arrow, and tried to pull it out, and would have done so, but the arrow was edged and cut and disabled his hand. He kept calling out that they should carry him back into the heat of the battle to encourage his soldiers, who very bravely disputed the fight without him, until night parted the armies. To his philosophy he owed the singular contempt he had for his life and for all human things. He had a firm belief in the immortality of souls.

In matters of religion he was wrong throughout, and was surnamed the Apostate for having abandoned ours; nevertheless, the opinion seems to me more probable that he had never thoroughly embraced it, but had dissembled out of obedience to the laws, until he came to the empire. He was so superstitious in his own religion that he was laughed at for it even by those of his own time who held the same opinion, who jeeringly said that if he had won his victory over the Parthians, he would have destroyed the breed of oxen in the world to supply his sacrifices. He was, moreover, besotted with the art of divination, and gave authority to all sorts of predictions. He said, among other things at his death, that he was obliged to the gods, and thanked them, in that they had not chosen to cut him off by surprise — having long before warned him of the place and hour of his death — nor by a mean and unmanly death more becoming to lazy and delicate people, nor by a lingering, long, and painful one; and that they had thought him worthy to die in this noble manner, in the midst of his victories, in the flower of his glory. He had a vision like that of Marcus Brutus, that first threatened him in Gaul and later appeared to him in Persia just before his death. The words some put in his mouth when he felt himself wounded — "Thou hast overcome, Galilean," or as others have it, "Be content, Galilean" — would hardly have been omitted, had they been believed, by my witnesses, who, being present in the army, set down the least motions and words at his end; any more than certain other miracles that are reported about it.

To return to my subject: he long nourished paganism in his heart, says Marcellinus; but since his whole army was Christian, he did not dare to declare it. In the end, seeing himself strong enough to dare to reveal himself, he had the temples of the gods thrown open, and did his utmost to set on foot and encourage idolatry. To do this the better, finding at Constantinople the people disunited, and also the prelates of the church divided among themselves, he called them all before him and earnestly urged them to calm those civil dissensions, and let every man freely, and without fear, follow his own religion. This he the more zealously solicited in hope that the licence would augment the schisms and factions of their division, and prevent the people from uniting, and so fortifying themselves against him by their unanimous understanding and concord — having found by the cruelty of certain Christians that there is no beast in the world that man has more cause to fear than man. These are very nearly his own words.

It is worth considering here that the Emperor Julian used the same recipe of liberty of conscience to inflame civil dissensions that our kings use to extinguish them. So one may say, on one side, that to give the people the reins to entertain every man his own opinion is to scatter and sow division, and as it were lend a hand to multiplying it, there being no legal impediment or restraint to stop or hinder its career; but on the other side, one may also say that giving the people the reins to entertain every man his own opinion is to soften and calm them by easiness and tolerance, and to blunt the point that is sharpened by singularity, novelty, and difficulty. And I think it better for the honour of the devotion of our kings that, not having been able to do what they would, they have made a show of being willing to do what they could.
